1:
Before a word of the psalm is expounded the witnesses linger over its puzzling superscription, To the chief Musician upon Gittith, A Psalm of David. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry records Dr. Hammond's conjecture that Gittith should be read "upon the Gittite," that is, Goliath of Gath, so that the psalm celebrates the enemy who was stilled by one who was, in comparison, but a babe and a suckling; yet Henry doubts the guess, since the same title stands over two other psalms, Ps. 81 and Ps. 84. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reports the old rendering "concerning the wine-presses," making it a psalm for the vintage season, while the Chaldee turns it "upon the harp which David brought out of Gath." The reformed John Calvin will not decide whether the word names an instrument, a tune, or some well-known song, but dismisses as strained and far-fetched the notion that the psalm was so called from the city of Gath.

The latin-fathers voice of Augustine takes the wine-press of the title spiritually, as he does the threshing-floor, for the Church, in which the good are for a time separated from the bad not in space but in affection, as corn is stripped of its chaff and wine of its husks. Turning to the opening cry, the witnesses admire how the address owns God twice over. Clarke parses "O Lord our Lord" as Jehovah our Adonai — from a root meaning to direct, rule, and support — so that the name tells both what God is in himself and what he is to man, our Prop and Stay. John Gill owns him simply the one God, Lord of all angels and men, and in a special manner the Lord and King of his saints; and Henry presses the possessive: if we believe God to be the Lord, we must avouch and acknowledge him ours, for he made us, protects us, and takes special care of us.

On "how excellent is thy name in all the earth" the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that here, for the first time in the Psalter, the poet's private feeling is swallowed up in a larger, human sense of God's relation to all mankind; the word the Authorized Version renders "excellent" the Septuagint and Vulgate make "wonderful," though he prefers "great" or "exalted." The closing clause, "who hast set thy glory above the heavens," Ellicott finds plainly corrupt and ungrammatical, the emendations many; he leans to Ewald's "Thou whose splendour is raised above the heavens," while owning that the poet may mean only the majesty of him whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain, as at 1 Kings 8:27. Henry hears in it the contrast of two worlds: on earth we only hear God's excellent name and praise it, while the angels above see his glory, and yet he is exalted above even their praise. Calvin adds that the "name" is no bare essence but the knowledge of God's character and perfections as he makes himself known. Already Clarke and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley hear the gospel in the verse — that a name once great in Israel only is now illustrious in all the earth shows, Wesley says, that the psalm speaks of the Messiah.
2:
The verse turns God's praise into a paradox — that he draws strength "out of the mouth of babes and sucklings" — and the witnesses work at both the wording and the persons meant. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott weighs the two renderings: the Septuagint's "thou hast perfected praise," quoted by our Lord at Matt. 21:16, catches part of the thought, that a child's simple wonder is the truest worship and that God works his greatest things by the weakest instruments; yet the martial language of the context, with its enemy and avenger, seems to him to demand the primitive sense of "strength" as a stronghold or defence — Ewald's "his merry babbling mouth provides a defence of the Creator against all the calumnies of the foe." Ellicott fixes the phrase too as "young children and sucklings," a set expression for the very young, and reads in a child's unspoilt innocence, as Wordsworth did, a proof of man's likeness to God.

Who these babes are the witnesses debate. The reformed John Gill will not take them for literal infants, though he grants the Jewish writers do, and though the marvel of the nursing child has often been urged; he reads them figuratively of the apostles and first preachers of the gospel, men who were babes and sucklings in their own eyes and the world's. Clarke finds the prophecy's first fulfilment in the Jewish children who cried "Hosanna to the Son of David" in the temple, the enemy and avenger being the chief priests and scribes offended at their cry; yet he also dwells, with wonder, on the sheer mechanism by which an infant draws its first milk, calling it the very finger of God, an argument to still every atheist. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers all three: the care of helpless children in the kingdom of nature, God's use of weak instruments in providence, and, in the kingdom of grace, the apostles — unlearned and ignorant men — by whom the devil's kingdom was thrown down.

On the closing purpose, "that thou mightest still the enemy and the avenger," Ellicott notes that the last word means properly him who avenges himself, while Henry names the great enemy the devil, whose oracles were silenced when the gospel was preached. The puritan-evangelical C.H. Spurgeon rounds the verse into a history: the lisping utterances of babes refute the learned fools who deny that there is a God, and the children who cried "Hosanna" in the temple, when proud Pharisees stood silent, were answered by the Saviour out of this very verse. The witnesses divide only over the register — whether the strength ordained be a stronghold reared against God's foes or the perfected praise of childish lips — but they agree that the Almighty is most glorified when his defence is raised from the weakest of his creatures.
3:
The psalmist lifts his eyes to "the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars," and the witnesses are quick to ask why the sun goes unmentioned. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry supposes the meditation was framed on a night-walk by moonlight, when the sun was not in view; and he draws from man's upward gaze a dignity, that where the beasts are made to look downward, man is made erect to look toward heaven and set his affections above. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke makes the omission deliberate art: had the sun appeared, the moon and stars could not have shown, and to have named it among them would have been as absurd in astronomy as a false perspective; against Bishop Horsley and Kennicott, who would restore the sun to the text, he insists that "the Spirit of God is always right." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion by another road: the very silence about the sun proves the psalm a hymn of the night.

The phrase "the work of thy fingers" the witnesses handle two ways. Henry hears in it the ease of omnipotence: the stretching out of the heavens needed no outstretched arm, but was done as a fine and curious piece of work is wrought with the fingers. Clarke, on the contrary, piles up the immensities of the planets and the sun — bulks thousands of times greater than the earth — only to marvel the more that such globes are called the work of God's fingers, an image he thinks more sublime even than the prophet's weighing of the mountains in scales at Isa. 40:12. On "which thou hast ordained," Ellicott glosses the word as "founded" or created, yet welcomes the English "ordained" for the order it imports into the cosmos; Clarke renders it "prepared and established," the spheres fitted to their places in number, weight, and measure.

The witnesses see the verse not resting in the stars but moving through them toward man. Henry makes the whole survey a preface to wonder: when we consider how God's glory fills the upper world, we may well marvel that he should stoop to notice so mean a creature as man, a thought he carries into v.4. Keil and Delitzsch order the grammar to the same end, taking this verse as the protasis — "as often as I gaze at thy heavens" — whose principal clause is the astonished question that follows. The puritan-evangelical C.H. Spurgeon draws the moral that a survey of the heavens abases the pride of man, that puny worm of the dust who yet struts in the haughtiness of his shame. So the moon and stars, by their very greatness, prepare the descent to the little creature whom God nevertheless crowns.
4:
"What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" — the wondering question is the hinge of the psalm, and over the man it means the witnesses divide most sharply. The reformed John Gill will have it none but Christ: the word Enosh names a frail, weak, mortal man, and so cannot be Adam in innocence, nor can it be Adam's whole posterity, since all things are not put under them; it is the man Christ Jesus, a worm and no man, a man of sorrows subject to death, of whom it was a marvel that God should be mindful. Against so exclusive a reading stand the grammatical-historical witnesses. Charles Ellicott takes the verse for man as man, poised between the two poles of human frailty and human glory — "the grandeur and the littleness, the excellence and the corruption," in Pascal's words — and contrasts the Hebrew's confidence with the modern poet's "sad astrology." Keil and Delitzsch likewise read a real man, a king soon to be given a kingdom.

Between these lies a mediating reading. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes the verse of both at once: first of mankind in general, the worm who is yet the darling of Providence, made but a little lower than the angels; and then, "in a particular manner," of Jesus Christ, in whom the apostle expounds it at Heb. 2:6-8. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the verse, for the moment, upon fallen man — "wretched, miserable man, in his fallen state, full of infirmity, ignorance, and sin" — and reads God's "visiting" him as the work of the Holy Spirit, who convinces of sin and keeps man in a salvable state. The two words are weighed as well as the two natures: Enosh, the frail creature, and "son of man," ben Adam, the child of the first rebel, or, as Ellicott has it, of merely human ancestry.

So the division is genuine, and it will run through the next three verses. Is the "man" whom God so honours the literal son of Adam, crowned at creation and celebrated in his frailty and dignity together, as Ellicott, Keil and Delitzsch, and Calvin read him? Or is he the second Adam, the man Christ Jesus, of whom alone the psalm's high words are strictly true, as Gill maintains and as the Epistle to the Hebrews and 1 Cor. 15:27 apply them? Henry's answer, that both senses stand — the literal fulfilled and transcended in the Messianic — is the road most of the witnesses finally walk, holding that the greatest honour ever done to human nature was that Christ should assume it. What none of them doubts is the wonder itself: that the God whose glory is above the heavens should be mindful of so small a thing as man.
5:
The clause "thou hast made him a little lower than the angels" turns, the witnesses see, on a single Hebrew word, and they do not read it alike. The reformed John Gill notes that the text says not "angels" but Elohim, which usually signifies "than God," and refers the verse to the human nature of Christ, made but a little lower than God in its near union with the Son. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke renders it frankly "thou hast lessened him for a little time from God," or made him less than God for a season, and sends the reader to his fuller notes on Heb. 2:6. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott grants that Elohim can name a class of supernatural beings, angels as well as God, but finds nothing in the context to limit it to angels; the plain sense, he says, is that God has made man "want but a little from God," that is, little less than Divine, and the Authorized Version follows the Septuagint — which the Epistle to the Hebrews in turn adopts — only to tone down an expression about man that seemed too bold.

A second question is whether the "little" measures degree or time. Clarke and the puritan-evangelical C.H. Spurgeon both hear a note of time: man is lowered but for a little while, and in Christ this was accomplished, who was made lower than the angels "by the suffering of death" and is now raised above them. Spurgeon adds the difference of nature — the angels are immortal, and man for a season is not — yet holds that when time is over the saints are no longer lower than they. On "crowned him with glory and honour" Ellicott offers the alternative "compassed," while Henry, from the previous verse, had found man's crown in his reason and his rule, the noble faculties that fit him to govern the creatures.

Here the larger debate presses hard. Gill and Spurgeon read the verse through the humiliation and exaltation of Christ, who for a little was made lower and then crowned Lord of all. Ellicott, keeping the psalm's own horizon, makes its theme the essential greatness of man, his moral sense and spiritual likeness to God, and hears the poet look past the bright stars to "a higher kinship with God himself." Yet the readings are not so far apart as they seem, for even those who take the verse first of man own that its full weight is only borne by the man Christ Jesus, in whom the honour lost by the first Adam is more than restored. Whether Elohim be God or the angels, and whether the abasement be of rank or of time, the witnesses agree that the verse crowns the frail creature of v.4 with a dignity next below heaven's own.
6:
With dominion the psalm reaches man's kingship, and the witnesses press the sweep of "thou hast put all things under his feet." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch hear behind the words the grant of Gen. 1:26, the "put under his feet" sounding like a paraphrase of the dominion there given; the "all" is unlimited in itself, as at Job 42:2 and Isa. 44:24, though the psalm's own expansion in the next verses reaches only to the creatures of land, air, and sea. Man, they say, is a king, and not a king without a territory. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dates man's charter from his creation and its renewal after the flood at Gen. 9:2: all the creatures are delivered into his hand, put under his feet not for their labour only but for their very lives, so that every time we partake of fish or fowl we realize the dominion given us over the works of God's hands.

But the reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke will not let the verse rest on the first Adam. Gill points out that the words are far larger than Adam's grant: all power in heaven and earth was given to Christ when he rose and ascended, so that even the angels are among the works put under his feet — the Ethiopic, he notes, reads "all the works of thy hands." Clarke is blunter still: though the brute creation was made subject to Adam, it could never be said of him that God had put all things under his feet; this is literally true only of the Lord Jesus, who emptied himself and was afterward highly exalted, and to whom the apostle applies the words at Phil. 2:6-9.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, by contrast, keeps to the rapturous survey of animated nature and man's kingship over every created thing, pointing to St. Paul's elevation of the thought into a higher sphere at 1 Cor. 15:27. So the division of the earlier verses hardens here into two frames for one sentence: a literal dominion of man over the beasts, which the psalm plainly describes and Paul lifts higher, or a dominion so total — reaching even to angels — that it can only be Christ's. Henry, as before, holds both, reading the creatures' subjection as man's by creation and Christ's by right of his exaltation; even in the days of his flesh, he notes, the Lord gave specimens of that power, commanding the winds and seas and appointing a fish to pay his tribute. The witnesses leave the verse poised between the throne of Adam and the throne of the Son of Man, bidding us wait "till we see all things put under him."
7:
The catalogue of man's subjects begins near at hand, with "all sheep and oxen," and the witnesses read the ordered list as the map of a kingdom. The reformed John Gill glosses the pair as the tame creatures, useful to man for food and for clothing, the household wealth that lives closest to his door. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sorts the verse into its two ranks — first the domestic animals, and those employed in husbandry, and then, with the turn of the "yea, and," the beasts of the field, all the wild inhabitants of the forest that own man's mastery from farther off. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the same gradation and warm to it: the enumeration passes from the tame creatures to the wild, and the poet grows enthusiastic as he surveys this province of man's dominion, his lofty language answering to the greatness of the theme.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, expounding the sweep of creatures, marvels that man should master animals many of them far stronger and swifter than himself: the sheep and oxen he folds and feeds are his willing servants, but even the wild beasts, one way or another, he proves too hard for, so that every kind of beast and bird is tamed, as Jas. 3:7 attests. And he has liberty to use them as he has occasion — "Rise, Peter, kill and eat," as the voice bade at Acts 10:13 — so that the flocks and herds of this verse stand for the whole submission of the lower creation, delivered into man's hand not for labour only but for life.

Keil and Delitzsch lift the plain inventory toward its New Testament use. It is just this psalm, they observe — of which one would least have expected it — that the New Testament so often quotes of the Messiah, so that the Lord's own title "the Son of Man" leans no less upon these verses than upon Dan. 7:13, and the writer to the Hebrews builds on this dominion at Heb. 2:6-8. So even the sheep and oxen are drawn into the psalm's double reckoning: they are the literal subjects of the man God crowned, and they belong to the wider kingdom of the Son of Man under whose feet all things are at last to be put. The witnesses do not divide over the creatures themselves; they only weigh how far the enumeration reaches, whether to man's homely lordship over the flock or, through him, to the universal dominion of Christ.
8:
The kingdom widens to its farthest bounds — "the fowl of the air, and the fish of the sea" — the creatures most remote from man, and the witnesses follow the psalm to the horizon. The reformed John Gill recalls how God commands even the birds to serve his people, raining quails about the tents of Israel and sending ravens to feed Elijah, or loosing them again to punish his enemies. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke grounds the whole grant in the covenant with Noah: all these were given to man in the beginning, and he holds a general dominion over them still, since the fear of man is laid upon every beast and fowl and fish, all delivered into his hand at Gen. 9:2, to which he thinks the psalmist plainly refers.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the fish especially, which live in another element and "pass unseen through the paths of the seas," and yet, though many are stronger and swifter than he, cannot escape the arts by which man makes himself their master. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott prefers the poetry of the Authorized Version's "whatsoever passeth" to the flatter "the fish who pass," and hears in "the paths of the seas" an echo of Homer's watery ways. It is with this far-flung image, he notes, that the poem is bound together; for the repetition of its opening thought at the close is the one deliberate touch of art the psalm allows itself, its whole contents woven, as it were, into a wreath.

Clarke records too the older devotion that read these creatures as figures — the sheep for the harmless faithful, the labouring oxen for those who toil in the Church, the wild beasts for fierce tempers subdued, the birds and the very fish of the deep all put under the feet of the King Messiah — a spiritualizing he traces through Bishop Horne and an ancient Psalter. Whether taken so or plainly, the verse completes the circle of man's dominion, from the flock at his door to the fish in the unsearchable sea. And here the two readings that have run through the psalm meet again: the birds and fishes are the literal empire of the man God made a little lower than himself, and they are the outermost provinces of the Son of Man to whom, as 1 Cor. 15:27 declares, all things are made subject.
9:
"O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!" — the psalm ends where it began, and the witnesses hear in the returning refrain not mere repetition but proof. The reformed John Gill observes that the sense with which the psalmist set out has not faded but deepened, confirmed and increased by the very instances he was led to notice, so that he closes with the identical words he opened, the wonder of them heavier now than at the first. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch make the same point from the structure: having demonstrated that the name whose glory the heavens reflect is glorious upon earth as well, the poet can repeat his opening thought in a wider and more comprehensive meaning, and so weave his psalm together, as it were, into a wreath.

The puritan-evangelical C.H. Spurgeon catches the artistry exactly: like a good composer the poet returns to his key-note, falling back into his first note of wondering adoration, so that what he began as a bare proposition he now sets down as a proven conclusion, with a kind of quod erat demonstrandum. Between the two utterances of the refrain the whole demonstration has been made — the glory above the heavens, the strength out of the mouths of babes, the moon and the stars, the crowning of man, and his dominion over the works of God's hands — so that the closing cry rests upon evidence which the opening cry could only announce.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the refrain its gospel breadth: the name now excellent in all the earth is the name of Jesus, celebrated wherever his gospel is preached and carried by Bibles and missionaries to the utmost nations. Henry closes to the same note, that the earth has been honoured with the presence of the Redeemer and is still enlightened by his gospel and governed by his power. So the psalm that opened by owning God "our Lord" ends by owning him Lord of all the earth, and the debate over its middle verses — whether they sing the dignity of man or the glory of the man Christ Jesus — is gathered up in a single name that, once great in Israel only, is now excellent to the world's ends. The witnesses part as they met, in wonder that so exalted a Lord should be, in covenant, ours.
